RP-8

 

RP-9               Delegations during the election period

Author:          Peter Thompson 

         

 

Summary:

In 2016 the NSW Government changed the Local Government Act to remove elected members from exercising any functions of the elected body from the date of the ordinary election until the date when the first meeting of the new Council is held. The change only applies to Councils where the Mayor is elected by Councillors which includes Wagga. In our case it means no elected member will exercise the functions of the elected body in the period between 4 December 2021 to the 10 January 2022. The purpose of this report is to recommend that Council delegate these functions to one of the elected members for the period 4 December 2021 to 10 January 2022.

 

 

Recommendation

That Council:

a       delegate to [insert name] the functions of the role of mayor as described in s226 from 4 December 2021 until the first meeting of the Council elected at the 4 December 2021 election

b       confirms that the delegation described in (a) shall cease when a Mayor is elected at the first meeting of the newly elected Council

c        confirms that this delegation shall be limited by the restrictions on delegations identified in s377 of the Local Government Act 1993

 

 

Report

When the current Local Government Act commenced in 1993 it included a section which prescribed the term of office of mayor. It prescribed that the term of office of a mayor ends when their successor is elected to that office.

 

For over a quarter of a century this provision was applied according to its terms at all local government authorities across the State. The key significance of the provision is that the Local Government tier of government is never without an elected member exercising the roles and functions of the elected body. This all makes sense as Local Government, like all other tiers of government in Australia, is led by members of the community elected to office.

 

While all Councillors cease to hold that civic office on the day of the next occurring ordinary election, the provision in the Act identified above made it clear that the civic office of mayor continued until a successor is elected.

 

In 2016, the NSW State Government amended the Local Government Act (The Act). The amendment did not change the section which provides that the civic office of the Mayor continues until a successor is elected. That section remains the same and in accordance with s230 of the Act, the term of Mayor still continues until a successor is elected.

Unfortunately, the operation of s230 has been disabled by an amendment made to a different section in the Act. The amendment introduced a subclause to the section which deals with casual vacancies in the civic office of councillor. The effect of the subclause is that any civic office of Mayor elected by Councillors (i.e. 92 councils in the State) also becomes vacant when the Mayor stops holding the civic office of Councillor. This happens on the day of the ordinary election. For the remaining councils in NSW with Mayors elected by popular vote there is no change, and those areas continue to have an elected member at all times.

 

For the other 92 councils, the change means that there is no person elected at an ordinary election performing the functions of the elected body between the date of the election and the first meeting of the new Council.

 

This change has caught councils by surprise. It is fair to say that there is outrage across many local government areas that the NSW State Government could remove the elected membership of local government in the way it has been done.

 

The NSW Government has so far steadfastly refused to reverse the change. The reasons for this position include the following:

 

If the view were to be taken that mayors elected by councillors should continue to hold their office as mayor until their successor is elected at the first meeting after the ordinary election, even where that person ceases to hold elected office in the Council at the election, this leads to a range of perverse outcomes. It would potentially allow a person who was not re-elected as a councillor at an ordinary election to:

 

·    Exercise any functions delegated to the mayor by the previous council

·    Exercise the policy making functions of the council in cases of necessity (section 226)

·    Preside as chair of the first meeting of the council until a new mayor is elected and

 

It is not relevant to this report to explore the merit of these reasons or the claim that they are perverse outcomes.

 

The Office of Local Government (OLG) have confirmed that Council has a power of delegation which can be used to delegate the functions of the role of Mayor to the current Mayor between the date of the election and the date of the first meeting of the new Council (copy of the OLG commentary is attached). Indeed, this delegation can be given to any person whatsoever.

 

Reconciling this position with the OLG’s first perverse outcome of a mayor elected by councillors continuing to hold civic office, as identified in the first bullet point above is also beyond the scope of this report and the abilities of the author.

 

The purpose of this report is to recommend that Council delegate the role and functions of Mayor to one of your number to be exercised between the date of the ordinary election and the first meeting of Council.

 

While the OLG recommends this delegation be given to the General Manager, it is the author’s view that this is not appropriate.

 

The Local Government Act has been crafted to recognise the role of elected members and the separate and distinct role of the bureaucracy. This distinction has a democratic pedigree that should not be disrupted.

 

Financial Implications

The recommendation includes delegating powers, authorities, duties or functions with potential financial implications, including the incurring of expenditure, between 4 December 2021 and 10 January 2022.

 

It is not proposed that any payment will be made to the person holding the delegation.

Policy and Legislation

Local Government Act 1993 (NSW)

 

Link to Strategic Plan

Risk Management Issues for Council

If an individual exercises functions which mirror the functions of the mayor (without being elected as a councillor) after the ordinary election, this would mean a person not elected to Council could exercise significant functions including, in cases of necessity, policy-making functions of Council.

Internal / External Consultation

This item was raised with the Audit, Risk and improvement Committee at their meeting on 7 October 2021. The Chairperson Report notes that, whilst it was beyond the scope of the Committee to fully consider the matter, discussion from members indicated concern with practices that are contrary to good governance. The discussion included concerns in relation to any proposal that delegations be exercised by those who are not a council official in particular.

 

Consultation was also undertaken with Office of Local Government NSW, LGNSW and Riverina Joint Organisation.

Councillor T Koschel requested advice on notification provisions for Development

Applications, in particular provisions relating to neighbouring properties.

Notification provisions for Development Applications including provisions relating to neighbouring properties

 

Council’s Notification Policy with regard to the assessment and determination of Development Applications is contained at Section 1.10 of the Wagga Wagga Development Control Plan (DCP) 2010. For the information of Councillors, a link to the relevant section of the DCP 2010 is provided below.

 

https://wagga.nsw.gov.au/__data/assets/pdf_file/0018/112248/ECM_2089515_v21_Version-Control-Project-Wagga-Wagga-DCP-2010-as-amended-Section-1-General-Version-23.pdf

 

The provisions of this section of the DCP 2010 set the minimum level for neighbour and stakeholder notification. The provisions of Section 1.10 are best described as a 4 step process as detailed below.

 

Step 1 - Development not requiring notification (or advertising)

Development identified under this part of Section 1.10 does not require notification (or advertising) by virtue of its low environmental impact and includes:

·    Single storey residential dwellings and alterations and additions (compliant with DCP and LEP provisions).

·    Outbuildings in association with existing dwellings not on flood prone land or within the heritage conservation area.

·    Outbuildings/farm buildings on rural zoned land (not flood prone or heritage listed)

·    Minor temporary events

·    Minor signage

The notification requirements for development that falls outside of Step 1 is then determined as per the provisions of Tables 1 and 2 as follows. The tables are to be read in order – i.e. if the proposal falls within both tables then table 1 is the relevant table.

 

Step 2 – Table 1

Table 1 identifies the notification and advertising requirements for the following types of development:

 

·  Heritage sites and Conservation area

·  Prohibited Developments

·  Existing uses

·  Alterations and additions

·  Special Purpose Zone development

·  Natural Waterways and Recreational Waterway Zone development

·  Subdivision

·  High impact telecommunication facilities

·  Extension hours of operation - licenced premises

·  Rural Fire Shed

 

An excerpt from this table follows.

 

The extent of notification to adjoining owners is determined as either Type A or Type B as described below:

 

If the development is not covered in Table 1, notification requirements are determined by Table 2 as follows.

 

Step 3 – Table 2

This table covers all of the land use definitions contained within the dictionary of the Wagga Wagga local Environmental Plan (LEP) 2010 and identifies the notification requirements for the development depended on what zone it is located within.  The following in an excerpt of the table demonstrating its format. For example, the requirements for an animal boarding establishment proposed within the RU1 Primary Production zone is identified in the red circle – code YB14.  The codes are explained in the key the table

 

Step 4 – Officer discretion

There may be occasions when these minimum provisions outlined above are increased at the discretion of the Council, taking into account the specific circumstances of the application and the possible impact of an application.

 

Section 1.10 also outlines the procedures for advertising and notification as summarised below.

 

Advertised Procedures

Changes to legislation now require Council to advertise development via its website as opposed to publishing within a locally circulated newspaper.  In addition to this, a site notification sign is placed on site providing details of the development during the notification period.

 

Notification procedures

Notification letters are sent by Australia Post service to the current landowners of the affected properties (as determined above – Type A or B). \ Letters are also sent to “the occupier” of the property in the event that this is not the landowner.

 

Section 1.10 also details requirements for multi-tenanted properties including strata title and community title.

M-2                 Local Traffic Committee - Electronic Meeting - 9 September 2021 

Author:         Warren Faulkner 

         

 

Summary:

The Local Traffic Committee were provided with an electronic business paper on 7 September 2021 as part of their planned ordinary meeting scheduled for 9 September 2021 and asked to provide comment and/or feedback on the Council officer recommendations presented. 

The Minutes for this electronic meeting are attached for Councillors’ reference.

 

 

Committee Recommendation

That Council:

a       receive the minutes of the Local Traffic Committee Meeting held on 9 September 2021

b       install NO PARKING zone for 15m either side of the driveways to Lot 1 DP 285846 that service 320-350 Copland Street, East Wagga

c        install time restricted ½ hour parking in five car parking bays adjacent to number 68 Fernleigh Road in the Turvey Tops Shopping complex

 

 

Report

The Traffic Committee received an electronic business paper that included two reports, both of which were formal matters requiring Council consideration. A summary of each report is as follows.

 

RP-1 PROPOSED NO PARKING ZONES IN FRONT OF 320-350 COPLAND STREET, EAST WAGGA WAGGA

 

Background

The customer in this matter is the work health and safety officer for and on behalf of Royans, the business which occupies 330-340 Copland Street who raised the following concerns with Council’s Traffic Section via email;

 

“Royans Truck & Trailer Repairs…would like to request Wagga Wagga Council to help us keep our workers and customers safe and members of the public. Due to trucks and trailers being parked along the street which are not from us it has obscured the view on driving out of our driveway causing several near misses. We actually had a very close one last week one of our foreman nearly got hit by a truck. We have asked one of the companies not to park there trucks to close and they understood but then some else just goes and parks there. Currently we have to slowly creep up and make a run for it. So we would like the Wagga Wagga Council to consider implementing some kind of parking restriction. We are happy to be flexible and even have no parking in business hours between the hours of 7am-6pm Mon-Fri.”

 

Comment

Traffic Officers met with the customer on site to discuss the concerns raised and to identify possible solutions. The most appropriate solution agreed upon was to restrict parking for 15 metres on either side of each driveway by the installation of RS-40 series No Parking signs as depicted in the diagram.

 

RP-2 PROPOSED HALF HOUR PARKING ADJOINING 68 FERNLEIGH ROAD IN THE TURVEY TOPS SHOPPING COMPLEX

 

Background

The operator of the Turvey Tops newsagency has requested council consider half hour time restricted parking for the five parking bays that front the newsagent and post office on the western side of the Turvey Tops Shopping centre carpark. These parking bays are currently unrestricted, and vehicles are parked for extended periods to access the neighbouring hotel and shopping complex, both of which are serviced by the Turvey Tops carpark. Vehicles are often parked for lengthy periods during weekdays and all day on weekends after vehicles have been left overnight and retrieved late the following day.

 

Comment

The nature of these businesses is reliant on regular turnover and the installation of time restricted parking in this location is consistent with recent decisions in respect of similar business operations at other locations in the city. The recommendation would require installation of the following signs R5-1-1L and R5-1-1-R depicting the words ½ P 6am-6pm Mon-Sat as depicted in the diagrams.
